items.prompt: Define a brief, and name its parts.
items.canonical_answer: A brief is the specification a piece of writing must fulfil: its form, audience, purpose, role and any focus the prompt adds. Every part is a requirement, and the piece is judged against the whole specification — which is why the brief is read twice and its five parts are written down before the first sentence.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the specification the piece must fulfil.
The five parts — form, audience, purpose, role, focus — are what the definition is made of.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for decoding a brief, in order.
items.canonical_answer: First the form: what kind of text? Second the audience: who reads it? Third the purpose: what must it do? Fourth the role: who is speaking? Fifth the focus: what extra thing does the prompt demand? Five answers, written down, and the piece is planned before it is written — the order exists because each answer shapes the search for the next.
marking_guidance: Credit the five steps in order: form, audience, purpose, role, focus.
An answer that starts with the focus has decoded the extra requirement before the standard four.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a task’s form and its purpose, and how does the difference show in the writing?
items.canonical_answer: The form is the kind of container — speech, email, report — and the purpose is what the piece must do inside it — inform, persuade, describe. The difference shows in every choice: an informing speech signposts and explains, while a persuading one presses and asks, and two speeches in the same form with different purposes read as different kinds of writing. The test is to ask what the piece is doing to its reader, which the form alone never settles.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the container against what happens inside it.
Must say how the difference shows: the choices each purpose makes, visible at sentence level.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A prompt asks for a blog post describing a local market for visitors. Learner A writes a lively story about a day helping at a stall; Learner B writes a description of the market’s sights, sounds and smells, with a short greeting to readers. Which better fulfils the brief, and what is the case against the other?
items.canonical_answer: B fulfils the brief: the form is a blog post (greeting, direct address, informal register), and the purpose is description (sights, sounds, smells), so both parts of the brief are met. The case against A is that its form is a story: the day’s events are the container, and the description the brief asked for is only what happens to be inside it — however lively, it is a narrative, and the task’s form is part of its specification. However, A’s voice and detail would serve B’s piece well, which is worth saying: the error is in the shape, not the writing.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: B, with the reason drawn from form and purpose both being met.
Credit the case against A with its evidence: a story’s shape where a description was set, so the form is wrong.
However, the strongest answers note what A does have — a voice and detail — because the error is in the shape, not the quality.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A task sets a leaflet encouraging households to save water. A learner writes an essay about water scarcity, with no headings and no address to the reader. What has gone wrong, and how could the learner have caught it?
items.canonical_answer: The error is writing in a different form from the one set: the brief named a leaflet — with its headings, direct address, imperatives and call to action — and the learner produced an essay, which is a different container with different conventions. The learner could have caught it by decoding the brief before writing and testing the plan against the five parts: the form column would have said "leaflet", and the plan — introduction, argument, conclusion — would have visibly failed the test.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the form set was a leaflet, and an essay was written.
Must give the catch: decode the brief first and test the plan against the form named.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A debate brief sets "as the second speaker for the motion". The learner’s speech argues the motion well but never acknowledges that anyone opposes it. What part of the brief has been missed, and what does it cost?
items.canonical_answer: The missed part is the occasion: a debate, second speaker, is a role in an argument that has two sides, and the brief’s "for the motion" implies the existence of the against. A speech that argues its side without acknowledging the other treats a debate as a soapbox, and the cost is the task’s fit: the piece is a good argument in the wrong occasion, marked as a poorer fit to the brief. The fix is one paragraph of the other side, answered — the debate’s own shape.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the occasion missed, and what the role in it implies.
Must say the cost: a poorer fit to the task, and give the fix — the acknowledged, answered counterargument.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A prompt asks for a speech persuading parents to support a new club, and adds: "create a sense of shared excitement". The learner’s speech is orderly, reasonable — and flat. What has been missed, and why does it matter to the marks?
items.canonical_answer: The missed part is the focus sentence: "create a sense of shared excitement" is an extra requirement riding on the task, and a reasonable speech that creates none has answered the form and the purpose while leaving the prompt’s own emphasis undone. It matters because the table rewards the task achieved in full, and the focus is part of the task — its absence reads as the task only partly done, whatever the orderliness. The fix is to plan for the effect: shared excitement needs shared pronouns, a named shared past and a future the audience is invited into.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the focus sentence and its named effect missed.
Must say why it matters: the task is judged as achieved in full or in part, and then give the fix.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give a plan for sharing up to 400 words across a piece of writing.
items.canonical_answer: An opening of about fifty words, establishing the form and the voice. Two or three developed sections of about a hundred each, carrying the content with ideas developed — claimed, reasoned, exemplified. A close of about fifty that lands the purpose. The words are a budget, not a ceiling to bump against, and the budget is planned before the writing starts so that development has room.
marking_guidance: Credit each step of the plan: opening, sections, close, with their word shares.
The budget point — planned, not bumped against — is what makes the plan a plan.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why does a very short answer lose marks on this task, even when its sentences are good?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that development is part of achieving the task: the table rewards ideas developed — claimed, reasoned, exemplified, carried — and a very short answer has usually produced a list where the task wanted a carrying. Good sentences in an underdeveloped piece are good sentences in a task only partly achieved, and the mark reads the piece as a whole, not the sentences one by one. The 400 words exist so that ideas can be carried, not merely named.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: development is part of the task, and short answers cannot develop.
An answer about "looking lazy" has described the impression, not the mechanism.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What must the opening of a 400-word piece do?
items.canonical_answer: It must establish the form and the voice at once, so the reader knows what they are reading and who is speaking before the first section arrives: a speech greets its hall, an email finds its reader, a report states its subject and purpose. In a piece this short the opening is a fifth of the whole, so it cannot be a throat-clearing — the strongest openings are already doing the piece’s work while they establish it.
marking_guidance: Credit the features of the opening: form established, voice established, work already begun.
An answer about "being interesting" has described a quality, not the opening’s job.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes 210 words for a task that allows 400: "I said everything I needed to." What has the learner misunderstood about the task, and what would the extra space be for?
items.canonical_answer: The learner has misunderstood the task as a message to deliver rather than a piece to develop: the 400 words exist so that ideas can be carried — reasoned, exemplified, shown working — and 210 words has usually named them. The extra space would be for development: the reason behind the claim, the example that makes it concrete, the consequence that gives it weight, the sentence that addresses the reader’s doubt. Nothing in the piece "needed saying" is the point — the task needed it shown.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the task rewards development, not just coverage.
Must say what the space is for: reasons, examples, consequences — the carrying that the table rewards.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: This is the content: "The library will now stay open until 18:00 on weekdays, after a trial term, because 40 per cent more learners used it in the afternoons." Rewrite it for a speech to classmates, then for an email to a strict head teacher.
items.canonical_answer: For classmates: "Good news — the library’s ours till six now. The trial worked: forty per cent more of us were in there every afternoon, and the school noticed. So the extra hours stay. Use them." For the head: "Dear Dr Iipinge, I am pleased to report that the extended library hours have been confirmed for the coming year. The trial term showed a forty per cent increase in afternoon use, which indicates the change serves its intended learners; the new closing time of 18:00 will apply from the first week of term." (The facts are one set; the vocabulary, contractions, pronouns and structures are two, because the audiences differ.)
marking_guidance: Credit each step of the rewrite: the extract’s content carried across twice, because the words show the two audiences.
Credit the visible register change: contractions and direct address for the hall, formal closure and evidence-forward order for the head.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Read these two sentences about the same cancelled match, written for the purpose — A is for teammates, B is for the fixtures secretary: A: "It’s off — the pitch is a lake. Sunday, same time, bring towels." B: "Owing to waterlogging, the fixture is postponed. A revised date will follow." How does the change of audience work on the words?
items.canonical_answer: A contracts ("It’s off"), personifies the pitch as "a lake" for comedy and shared knowledge, and gives an instruction with a joke attached ("bring towels"), because teammates are friends who need the news and the mood. B subordinates the cause in a Latinate passive ("Owing to waterlogging"), removes every person from the sentence, and defers the remedy to the future ("will follow"), because a fixtures secretary needs a record and a chain of accountability, not the mood. The reader of A is a participant; the reader of B is a file — and every difference between the sentences follows from that.
marking_guidance: Must name the audience’s work on the words: contractions and personification against passive and Latinate vocabulary.
Must trace the effect on each reader: the friend gets the mood and the news, the official the record and the accountability.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between formal and informal register, and what decides which one fits a piece of writing?
items.canonical_answer: Formal register follows the conventions of formal public usage — no contractions, Latinate vocabulary, complete structures, no first-person asides; informal register follows casual private usage — contractions, everyday words, direct address, spoken markers. What decides which fits is the audience and the purpose, not a general ranking: a formal register suits an official reader and an official purpose, an informal one suits a friend and a friendly one, and each mismatches the other’s task as badly as the reverse. The question is not "which is better?" but "which reader, and for what?"
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: the two sets of features, public usage against casual usage.
Must give the decider: the audience and purpose as a pair, with the mismatch running both ways.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Define a reflective commentary, and state its marks.
items.canonical_answer: A reflective commentary is an analysis of your own writing’s choices of form, structure and language, judged against the brief — how the choices contributed to fulfilling it. It is not a summary of what the piece says, and it is worth ten marks on Paper 2 Question 1(b), all for the analysis: the same craft as the analysis of a stranger’s text, with your own under the lens.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: an analysis of your own choices against the brief.
The boundary — not a summary — and the ten marks are part of the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Why is a commentary analysis rather than a summary, and what does retelling fail to do?
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that the commentary’s reader already holds your piece: retelling tells them what they know, and the commentary’s job — the thing retelling fails to do — is to explain what the choices do, which the piece by itself does not show. "I opened with the noise of the market" retells; "I opened with the noise rather than the name so the reader stands inside the market before knowing where they are — the brief’s focus on atmosphere" analyses. The marks are for the second kind of sentence, because the second kind is the commentary.
marking_guidance: Credit the reason: the reader holds the piece, so explanation — not repetition — is what earns the marks.
The example pair, or its equivalent, shows the difference the answer is arguing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between what your text says and what your choices do, and which one is the commentary about?
items.canonical_answer: What your text says is its content — the events, facts and opinions it carries; what your choices do is the craft — how the form found the reader, how the structure carried them, how the language held them. The commentary is about the second, because the first is already on the page and the second is the thing a writer can explain that a reader cannot see. The test is the question every commentary sentence answers: what did this choice make happen for the audience and the brief?
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: content carried against craft at work.
Must say which the commentary is about, and give the test that keeps the sentences on it.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner’s commentary says: "My piece uses many good techniques which make it effective." What two things are wrong with the sentence, and what should replace it?
items.canonical_answer: The first wrong thing is the absence of quotation: "many good techniques" claims craft and quotes none of it, so no reader can check a word of the sentence. The second is the stock praise: "effective" could close a claim about any text ever written, which means it analyses nothing about this one. The replacement names the choice and quotes it: "the closing tricolon — ‘we came, we saw, we grew’ — gathers the term’s whole argument into the last line the hall hears, which serves the brief’s demand for a speech that persuades by momentum rather than instruction."
marking_guidance: Must name the error: no quotation, and stock praise that fits any text.
Must give the replacement: choice named, words quoted, effect tied to the brief.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the four moves of a commentary paragraph, in order.
items.canonical_answer: First the choice: which decision of form, structure or language is being explained. Second the quotation: the words of your own text that carry the choice, embedded in the sentence. Third the effect: what the choice makes the reader think, feel or do. Fourth the link to the brief: how the effect contributes to fulfilling the specification the piece was written to. Four moves, in that order, and the paragraph is a commentary rather than a diary.
marking_guidance: Credit the four steps in order: choice, quotation, effect, link to the brief.
The order matters because the quotation is the evidence the effect is built on.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a line from a learner’s speech: "Some of you have never known this school without the tuck shop." Write one commentary sentence on this line, in the four moves.
items.canonical_answer: A model sentence: "The direct address — ‘some of you have never known’ — makes the tuck shop’s closure sound like a shared history being taken away, which positions the hall as its defenders and serves the brief’s demand for a speech that persuades the school to keep it." (Any sentence that names the choice, quotes the words, states the effect on the hall, and links to the brief meets the task; the four moves are the shape.)
marking_guidance: Credit the sentence: the four moves in one commentary sentence, because the shape is the skill.
The quotation must be embedded in the sentence’s grammar, so the commentary shows the craft it claims.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A commentary reads: "I used adjectives, metaphors and alliteration, and also some short sentences." What is the learner doing, and what is missing from every sentence of it?
items.canonical_answer: The learner is feature-spotting in their own writing: a list of devices is named and none of them is quoted or explained, so the commentary claims craft and demonstrates none. What is missing from every sentence is the same pair: the words (the quotation that shows the choice) and the work (the effect the choice had on the audience and the brief). The fix is the four moves — choice, quotation, effect, link — run for each feature, and the list of four devices becomes four analysis sentences or none.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: features listed in the learner’s own writing, none quoted or explained.
Must give what is missing: the quotation and the effect, and the fix of the four moves.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A commentary says: "I used a lot of alliteration because it makes things sound nice." Why does this sentence earn almost nothing, and what would its earned version look like?
items.canonical_answer: The sentence earns almost nothing for two reasons: "because it makes things sound nice" is a stock effect that could attach to any alliteration in any text, so it analyses nothing about this one; and the claim of "a lot" quotes no words at all, so the reader cannot check the device exists. An earned version: "the alliterated pair ‘shelves and stories’ in the second paragraph turns the library’s two functions into one sound, so the reader hears them as inseparable — which serves the brief’s demand for a piece that makes the library matter to its users." The words are quoted, the effect is theirs, the link is to the brief.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: a stock effect and no quotation.
Must give the earned version: quotation, its specific effect, and the link to the brief.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What must a commentary cover, and why all of it?
items.canonical_answer: It must cover form, structure and language, each tied to the audience it serves, because the brief was fulfilled by all three working together: the form found the reader, the structure carried them, the language held them. A commentary that covers one ground has described a third of the achievement, and the table rewards the whole — so the plan has three headings before the writing starts, and no heading is left empty.
marking_guidance: Credit the three grounds: form, structure, language, each tied to its audience.
The reason — the brief was fulfilled by all three — is what the features are for.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the steps for sharing a commentary across form, structure and language.
items.canonical_answer: First, fix the headings: form, structure, language — three grounds, three paragraphs or sections. Second, fill the form paragraph from the piece’s conventions: the greeting, the salutation, the report’s sections — each choice, quoted. Third, fill the structure paragraph from its route: the opening’s promise, the order, the close. Fourth, fill the language paragraph or two from the register, the imagery and the sentence shapes that did work. The share is decided by where the choices sit — a piece with a clever frame and one striking image gives the frame its paragraph and the image its own.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps: headings fixed, then each ground filled from the piece’s own choices.
The share by choices — not by equal thirds — is what makes the plan honest.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A commentary explains the learner’s imagery in loving detail and never mentions the email’s subject line, its two-paragraph shape or its sign-off. What has been left out, and why does it cost marks?
items.canonical_answer: What has been left out is form and structure: the subject line is a form choice doing work for the reader who skims inboxes, the two-paragraph shape is a structural decision about how much the reader can absorb, and the sign-off is a form convention positioning the writer — all of them choices the brief was fulfilled by. It costs marks because the table rewards commentary on all three grounds, and a commentary on language alone has accounted for a third of the achievement; the plan with three headings exists precisely to prevent the empty one.
marking_guidance: Must name the error: the form and structure choices left out, with examples of each.
Must say why it costs: the table rewards all three grounds, and the three-heading plan is the cure.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Write a speech opening a class debate, as the first speaker for the motion that the school should make its own uniform policy, to the hall of learners and teachers, introducing both sides. The writing must introduce both sides of the question, and open the case for the motion. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
Good morning, teachers and learners. The motion before you today is that this school should make its own uniform policy, and I open the case for it by saying the quiet part: a uniform policy written by the people who wear the uniform will be a better policy than one written for them.
Let me be fair to the other side before I am unfair to them. The argument against is the argument you have already heard: uniforms create identity, equality and order, and a learner-made policy risks becoming a fashion show with committee minutes. I take that seriously, and I answer it this way: our case is not the abolition of the uniform. Our case is authorship.
Consider what our present policy actually is. It is eleven rules, drafted in 2011, three of which nobody can enforce, one of which bans a garment none of us own, and one of which — I quote our own student council minutes from that year — was described by the then head learner as ‘a rule about rules’. We wear the consequences of that drafting every summer.
A learner-written policy would not be a free-for-all. It would be negotiated with the school, published with its reasons, and reviewed every two years by the people it governs. Identity, equality and order — the other side’s three words — survive all of that, and grow stronger, because rules you helped write are rules you defend.
I will end where the debate should end: not with what we wear, but with who we are becoming. A school that trusts its learners to draft one policy is teaching citizenship in a uniform. I ask the hall to support the motion.
marking_guidance: Mark against the 15-mark table: one writing column, five strands.
Expression and range: credit assured expression drawing on a broad repertoire of structures and vocabulary, some complex or unusual — the model answer is the standard.
Accuracy: credit writing with very few errors, and the full range of the form’s conventions present and correct.
Organisation and development: credit a piece organised with clear logic and strong effect, its ideas developed with subtlety throughout — the opening, sections and close share the words well.
Task achievement and audience: the task achieved in full, everything relevant, and the audience held throughout — the brief’s form, purpose, role and focus all fulfilled.

A Level 3 answer would be clear and correctly formed, with some complex structures and suitable vocabulary, the task achieved and the audience addressed — but plainer, less varied, and less strongly held.

items.prompt: Part (b). Write the reflective commentary on your debate speech: how did its choices of form, structure and language go about fulfilling the brief — the form, the audience, the purpose, the role, and the focus "introduce both sides of the question, and open the case for the motion"? Support every point with words quoted from your own speech. [10]
items.canonical_answer:
My piece is a debate speech, and its brief asked me to open the case for a motion as the first speaker, introducing both sides — so my commentary explains how its choices of form, structure and language fulfilled that specification for the hall.

The form does the brief’s first job. The opening — “Good morning, teachers and learners” — greets the hall directly, and the announcement of the motion in the first sentence (“The motion before you today…”) establishes the debate convention before the argument, so the audience knows what they are hearing and the role in it, which the brief’s “as the first speaker” requires. The close — “I ask the hall to support the motion” — performs the debate’s own ritual and lands the purpose, because a debate speech that never asks for the vote is a speech, not a debate.

Structurally, the piece gives the opposition its paragraph second — “Let me be fair to the other side” — and answers it within the same paragraph, which fulfils the focus in the brief on introducing both sides while keeping my case in command of the order: the audience meets the counterargument through me, not after me. The two long middle paragraphs alternate evidence and refutation, and the quotation of the 2011 minutes (‘a rule about rules’) arrives at the argument’s centre so the hall has something memorable to carry into the vote.

The language holds the hall. The first-person plural — “our case is not the abolition of the uniform. Our case is authorship” — turns the motion into a shared identity, and the antithesis of the pair is the sentence I chose for the hall to repeat to itself; the conversational asides (“and I am being unfair to them” by implication, “the quiet part”) position me as candid rather than combative, which suits an audience of learners and teachers deciding a vote. Together the choices fulfil the brief: both sides introduced, the first speaker’s case opened, and the hall asked.
marking_guidance: Mark against the 10-mark table: one analysis column.

Credit assured analysis of the text’s form, structure and language, and of how the choices suit its audience and shape its meaning — the model commentary quotes the model piece in short embedded stretches and ties every point to the brief.
Credit the three grounds covered: form and its conventions, the structure’s route, and the language’s work — no ground left empty, each tied to the audience it serves.
Credit the four moves run repeatedly: the choice, the quotation from your own text, its effect on the reader, and the link to the brief.
Do not credit retelling of what the piece says, feature-listing without effect, or a commentary that quotes nothing.
A Level 3 commentary would be clear and coherent, quoting some choices and tying them to the audience — but covering the grounds unevenly and stating effects more generally.

items.prompt: Write a speech to parents at a school open evening, persuading them to support the new robotics club. The writing must create a sense of shared excitement about the club. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
Good evening, parents, and welcome. I am here tonight to ask you to support the new robotics club — and I want to begin with the shared excitement this club already has, because your children voted for it with their feet.
At the taster session last month, forty-one learners turned up for twenty places. They filled the corridor outside the lab. Two of them brought their own screwdrivers. One of them, a Grade 9 who has never voluntarily stayed late for anything, asked me whether the club could meet twice a week. That is the room I want to give you tonight — not a curriculum, but that corridor.
And here is my favourite part, the part that belongs to you. The club needs parents. Not as spectators: as builders, judges, drivers and tea-makers. The regional competition in May needs a minibus driver, three team mentors and an audience that claps loudly at the right moments. Last year’s pilot school found that the parents who helped were the ones who couldn’t tell a servo from a sandwich — and their learners told us it was the best term of the year, because for once the generations were learning the same thing in the same room, at the same speed.
So this is my ask, and it is a shared one: sign the list tonight, take the dates, and bring the whole household to the first open build on the ninth. Come and stand in that corridor. I promise you the excitement is catching, and I have forty-one witnesses.
marking_guidance: Mark against the 15-mark table: one writing column, five strands.
Expression and range: credit assured expression drawing on a broad repertoire of structures and vocabulary, some complex or unusual — the model answer is the standard.
Accuracy: credit writing with very few errors, and the full range of the form’s conventions present and correct.
Organisation and development: credit a piece organised with clear logic and strong effect, its ideas developed with subtlety throughout — the opening, sections and close share the words well.
Task achievement and audience: the task achieved in full, everything relevant, and the audience held throughout — the brief’s form, purpose, role and focus all fulfilled.

A Level 3 answer would be clear and correctly formed, with some complex structures and suitable vocabulary, the task achieved and the audience addressed — but plainer, less varied, and less strongly held.

items.prompt: Part (b). Turn analyst now: write the reflective commentary on your speech to the parents, explaining how your choices of form, structure and language fulfilled the brief — the form, the audience, the purpose, the role, and the focus "create a sense of shared excitement about the club". Quote your own words throughout. [10]
items.canonical_answer:
My piece is a speech to parents at a school open evening, and the brief asked me to persuade them to support the new robotics club with a sense of shared excitement — so this commentary explains how the form, structure and language did that persuading and built that excitement for this audience of parents.

The form addresses its audience from the start: “Good evening, parents, and welcome” finds the room before the ask, and the speech’s closing imperative — “sign the list tonight, take the dates” — gives the audience something physical to do, which is what a persuasive speech owes its occasion: the parents arrive as an audience and leave as participants. The ask is stated plainly (“my ask, and it is a shared one”), and its brevity against the paragraphs before it makes it easy to say yes to.

The structure builds the excitement the brief names. The opening’s anecdote — “forty-one learners turned up for twenty places”, the corridor, the screwdrivers — gives the excitement evidence rather than assertion, so the parents are shown the room before they are asked to join it. The second paragraph turns the audience into the solution: the club “needs parents”, the list of roles is concrete (driver, mentors, tea-makers), and the pilot school’s detail — parents who “couldn’t tell a servo from a sandwich” — removes the qualification barrier the audience might be raising against itself, which is the piece’s most persuasive structural move: the objection is answered before it is voiced.

The language makes the excitement shared. items.prompt: Write a story opening for a school anthology. The writing must create a sense of unease. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
The kettle had been talking to itself for an hour, and I had been too polite to listen.

It started at the switch. Not a sound the kettle had made before — a little click, then a hum that was not quite a hum, like something practising a sentence it would not be allowed to say. I put it down to the pipes. Our block is famous for its pipes; they hold conversations at night that the whole building pretends not to hear.

But the kettle kept talking, and at eleven at night, in a flat with thin walls and thinner explanations, a kettle that hums with intent is a different kettle from the one you bought. I made tea. The tea tasted fine. The tea is not the point of this story.

The point is the landing. I carried the mug out of the kitchen and the landing light was on, which it never is, and I stood there with the steam going up past my face thinking: who turned it on? And behind me — I want to be exact about this, because it was the last exact thing I felt — behind me, the kettle’s hum stopped. Not switched off. Stopped. The way a person stops talking when they realise someone else is in the room.

I stood there for a moment with my tea and my light and my very quiet kettle. Then I drank it, because I am not a coward, I am just a person who makes notes. And the kettle said nothing else all night, which was somehow worse.

The plumber came on Thursday. He found a loose element. He showed it to me. I thanked him. I have not used that kettle since.

items.prompt: Write a story opening for a magazine competition. The writing must create a sense of wonder. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
The heron was the first thing I ever saw that was better than a photograph.

I was eleven, on my grandfather’s pontoon on the Kavango, and the morning had already given us a kingfisher and a fish eagle and the kind of sunrise that postcards copy, and I was already thinking the day could not be improved. Then the heron came up out of the reeds like a folded letter opening, and everything I knew about birds was quietly rearranged.

I wish I could tell you the photographs did it justice. I have one, at home, framed: the heron mid-lift, the river glass-flat, the whole morning balanced on the bird’s one raised leg. It is a good photograph. It is not the thing. The thing had size, and silence, and the sense — I know I was eleven, but I have checked the feeling against every heron since — that I was in the presence of something that had decided to be seen.

That is the wonder, and I have been chasing it ever since. Not the bird — the being seen. Every heron since has been a message from that first one: look up, be quiet, wait. Sometimes I think my whole career in biology started because an eleven-year-old wanted to know what the heron knew.

It is my turn now to take learners out on the water. When the first heron comes up, I watch their faces, and I see it happen — the rearranging, the silence. And I say the only thing my grandfather said to me that morning, the words that have kept their wonder for thirty years: ‘It knows you’re here. Make it worth the look.’

items.prompt: Write a blog post about a skill you learned the hard way, encouraging others to try it. The writing must make the skill feel startable for a reader who has failed at it before. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
Nobody warns you that the hardest part of learning to drive is not the clutch. It is the sitting in a car park for the third week while a patient relative says ‘gently’ in a voice that has lost all meaning.

I learned the hard way, and I learned late, at twenty-three, which is old enough to be embarrassed and young enough to write about it. My teacher was my aunt, a woman who has driven everything from grain trucks to an ambulance, and whose calm I mistook, for two weeks, for approval. It was not approval. It was patience, which is what a saint has instead of opinions.

Here is what nobody tells you, the thing I needed to hear in that car park. The car will not move until your foot believes it can, and your foot believes what your hands and your eyes and your breathing tell it. So learn the feet first, in the quiet, with no traffic and no audience and no destination. Spend a whole session just finding the bite point, forward and back, five metres either way, until it is boring. Boring is the destination. When the bite point is boring, the rest of driving is a set of habits, and habits are learnable in a way that terror is not.

The second thing: find your aunt. Everyone learns faster with the right person in the passenger seat, and the right person is the one whose ‘gently’ you still respect at week three. Mine took me to the car park every Sunday for a month, then to the quiet streets, then to the road, and last year she let me drive her to the coast, and she said ‘gently’ only twice, and both times I needed to hear it.

Learn the feet. Trust the boring. And when your aunt falls asleep in the passenger seat on the coast road, you are a driver.

There is a moment, at about quarter past five, when this town belongs to the bakers.

I say this as a confirmed non-baker and a professional sleeper. You will find no one less qualified to praise the dawn than me. But I have now walked it every day for a month, because I promised this blog I would describe my town to visitors, and the town I most want to show you only exists for about forty minutes.

Start at the bridge, where the mist is still making up its mind. The river under it is the colour of a spoon — old silver, warm silver, the kind that has been in a family for generations. The first sound is not the birds, whatever the postcards say. It is the bakery on Kavii Street, whose ovens come on at four, and whose front door at half past five opens with a smell that travels: it meets you at the bridge, a full street away, and it walks you into town.

Down the main road, the shutters are going up in ones and twos. The fruit seller arranges her pyramid — it is a pyramid, she will tell you so — and the taxi rank wakes in stages, first the drivers, then the rank’s own particular argument about positions, which I have come to regard as the town’s alarm clock. By six, the light has reached the church roof, and it goes from grey to gold in the time it takes to cross the road.

Come and walk it. Set two alarms if you must — I did, every day for a week. And when you smell bread, at the bridge, a full street from its source, you will understand why I dragged you out of bed: the dawn here is not a view. It is an escort, and it walks you all the way in.

items.prompt: Write a report to the school board on how students use the library. The writing must give the board findings it can act on, with the recommendations costed. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
REPORT TO THE SCHOOL BOARD: LIBRARY USE, SPRING TERM

To: The Governing Board. From: The Library Working Group, March meeting.

Purpose and method. This term we monitored how, when and why learners use the library, using door counts for four weeks, a written survey completed by 212 learners, and interviews with staff who book the space. The findings below are the ones we ask the Board to act on.

Findings. First, the library is busiest when it is least expected: 58 per cent of visits happen between 13:10 and 14:00, when the space is supervised by one teacher and every table is full. Second, the library is used far more for group work than its layout allows — 47 per cent of surveyed learners come to work with classmates, and the survey’s most common written comment (31 separate times) is some version of ‘we need to be able to talk quietly’. Third, fiction borrowing is rising steadily, up a fifth on last year, and the waiting list for the three most popular series now runs to six weeks.

What this suggests. The library is not short of learners; it is short of room, of layout and of stock. The demand at lunchtime exceeds a single supervisor’s safe capacity; the furniture prevents the group work most learners come for; and the fiction shelves are being read faster than the budget replaces them.

Recommendations. (1) A second supervisor for the lunchtime period, costed by the working group at N$2,800 per term, which we regard as the report’s most urgent item. (2) A trial rearrangement of the west tables over the coming holiday into four group bays, at no cost beyond staff time. (3) An increase of N$4,000 to the fiction budget, to cut the six-week waiting list to two.

We are content to present any of this in person, and we ask the Board to note item (1) before the new term begins.

items.prompt: Write a leaflet encouraging households to cut food waste. The writing must make the changes feel doable for busy people, and give them a first step. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
The leaflet on my fridge says we each throw away a plate of food a day. A plate. Every day. I checked — because that number should be impossible in a country where grandmothers can still remember a bad harvest — and it is not just possible: our household was doing it.

So here is what changed, in the order it changed, because this is a leaflet for busy people and not a confession. First, the shopping list. We began planning the week’s meals on Sunday evening, and the rule is one simple thing: write the list after the plan, not before the walk. That one change cut our waste by what feels like half, and I am told by people who measure these things that it is the change every kitchen makes first.

Second, the fridge shelf. Everything that must be eaten soonest lives at eye level, in a container, with a label and a date; everything long-lasting lives lower down. The forgotten yoghurt at the back — we all have one — stopped existing, because the back of our fridge is now a place nothing is exiled to.

Third, and this is the one your grandmother already knew: cook once, eat twice. Sunday’s stew is Tuesday’s filling, and Tuesday’s filling is Wednesday’s soup with a handful of rice. The pot that ends the week is the pot that started it, and it is better at the end.

None of this is hard. All of it saves money — our food bill dropped by a fifth in the first month, which is the kind of arithmetic that keeps a habit going. Start with the list. The plate you save is your own.

items.prompt: Write a letter to a newspaper, responding to the claim that young people do not read. The writing must answer the claim with evidence, and concede what is true in it. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
Dear Editor,

Your correspondent last week claimed that young people ‘do not read’, and I would like to answer the claim with our library’s own numbers, since I am one of the young people in question and I have been counting.

Our school library issued 4,118 books last year. Of those, 3,203 went to learners — and fiction borrowing is rising, not falling, up a fifth on the year before, with a waiting list for the most popular series that runs to six weeks. Six weeks, for a book. Your correspondent’s generation queued for bread with less patience than my classmates queue for a fantasy trilogy.

What has changed is not whether we read. It is what we read, and how. Your correspondent laments the death of ‘long’ reading; my classmates and I have read more words this year than any generation before us — on screens, admittedly, which appears to be the objection, as though the value of a sentence depends on the material beneath it. We read news, we read argument, we read each other’s writing constantly. The novel has not died; it has moved in next door to everything else.

And here is my evidence that the love of reading is alive, because I promised you numbers and not nostalgia: our book club, founded by learners two years ago, has forty-three members and a rule that you finish the book. We have read eleven novels this year. Your correspondent is welcome at any meeting — the door is open, the discussion is loud, and the reading is long.

Perhaps the claim should be narrowed: young people do not read the way their parents did. Fair. We read more.

Yours faithfully,
K. Uugwanga, Grade 12

items.prompt: Write a diary entry on the evening of your first day in a new job. The writing must record the day honestly, at its true size, and mark what has changed. Use no more than 400 words. [15]
items.canonical_answer:
Dear diary — and I am aware I have not written in you since the last crisis, which tells you what kind of day this has been.

I got the job. I keep typing that sentence and deleting it, which is the day in miniature: nothing feels finished, everything is at once too big and too small to say. I got the job. The call came at 11:40 while I was carrying shopping, and the manager talked for two minutes about the team and the rota and the probation period, and I said ‘thank you’ nine times, which I have now counted on the recording I apparently made of myself saying thank you nine times to a voicemail.

The first day was today, and I want to record three things while they are still true. One: nobody expects you to know where anything is. I asked where the kettle was four times, and by the fourth time it was a joke, and by lunch I had a nickname, which at my age and in my terror was the greatest gift the day gave me. Two: the work is easy and the not-knowing is hard. The gap between them is where I live at the moment, and I am told by the kind people who have done this before that the gap closes at about week three, and I am writing that down so that future me can check.

Three: I walked home the long way, past the harbour, and I felt — this is the sentence I deleted twice already — I felt like a person who had started something. Not finished. Started. The money is small, the title is smaller, and the shoes I bought for the interview have already given me a blister that I refuse to discuss.

Tomorrow I will write something more useful. Tonight I am just glad, in a room with one working bulb, about a job in a hardware shop, and about the fact that at 11:40 this morning, while holding a bag of bread and saying thank you to nobody, my whole life turned on a kettle question nobody was really asking me.
